content.text: {"primary_meaning":"In mainstream Christian teaching, 'life' or 'the life' symbolically denotes eternal, divine life (Greek zoe) that comes from God and is embodied in and given through Jesus Christ — a qualitatively new spiritual existence in communion with God, as opposed to mere biological existence (bios) or spiritual death. In Johannine usage especially, Christ himself is identified as 'the life,' so the term functions both as the gift (eternal life for believers) and the giver (Christ as the source and embodiment of that life).","primary_basis":["John 14:6 — 'I am the way, and the truth, and the life'","John 11:25 — 'I am the resurrection and the life'","John 1:4 — 'In him was life, and the life was the light of men'","John 3:16 — 'whoever believes in him should not perish but have eternal life'","John 5:26 — 'as the Father has life in himself, so he has granted the Son also to have life in himself'","John 10:10 — 'I came that they may have life, and have it abundantly'","John 17:3 — 'this is eternal life, that they know you, the only true God, and Jesus Christ'","1 John 5:11-12 — 'God gave us eternal life, and this life is in his Son; whoever has the Son has life'","1 John 1:1-2 — 'the word of life... the life was made manifest'","Colossians 3:4 — 'Christ who is your life'","Romans 6:4 — 'walk in newness of life'","Galatians 2:20 — 'it is no longer I who live, but Christ who lives in me'"],"alternatives":[{"meaning":"Christ himself as 'the Life' — a personal, christological identification rather than a state or gift; life is not a thing bestowed but a Person indwelling the believer (emphasized in Johannine theology, patristic writers, and traditions such as the deeper-life and Watchman Nee/Witness Lee streams).","basis":["John 14:6","John 11:25","Colossians 3:4","Galatians 2:20","Philippians 1:21"],"prominence":"common"},{"meaning":"Eternal life as post-mortem immortality — everlasting existence in heaven after death, emphasizing future duration rather than present quality; common in popular piety though many scholars stress that Johannine eternal life is a present possession.","basis":["John 3:16","Matthew 25:46","Daniel 12:2","Romans 6:23"],"prominence":"common"},{"meaning":"Abundant life — a present-tense quality of flourishing, fullness, blessing, and vitality in this world; in some prosperity-oriented teaching this extends to material and physical well-being.","basis":["John 10:10","Deuteronomy 30:19-20","Psalm 16:11"],"prominence":"common"},{"meaning":"Life as participation in the divine nature (theosis/divinization) — sharing in God's own uncreated life; emphasized in Eastern Orthodox theology.","basis":["2 Peter 1:4","John 5:26","John 6:53-57","1 Corinthians 15:45"],"prominence":"minority"},{"meaning":"Life as breath/soul (Hebrew nephesh, ruach) — the animating principle given by God, a natural rather than symbolic sense stressed in Old Testament scholarship; sometimes linked to 'the life is in the blood.'","basis":["Genesis 2:7","Leviticus 17:11","Job 33:4","Ecclesiastes 12:7"],"prominence":"common"},{"meaning":"Life mediated through symbols of access — the tree of life, bread of life, water of life, and book of life — where 'life' names covenantal fellowship with God restored in the new creation.","basis":["Genesis 2:9; 3:22-24","John 6:35","Revelation 2:7; 21:6; 22:1-2","Revelation 20:15"],"prominence":"common"},{"meaning":"Conditionalist/annihilationist reading — 'life' means literal continued existence itself; the alternative to eternal life is cessation of being rather than eternal conscious torment.","basis":["John 3:16 ('perish')","Romans 6:23","Matthew 10:28"],"prominence":"minority"}],"has_settled_consensus":true,"confidence":"high","notes":"There is broad, recognizable consensus across Catholic, Orthodox, and Protestant traditions that 'life/the life' in the New Testament symbolizes eternal, divine (zoe) life found in Christ — both a present spiritual reality and a future consummation — with Christ himself identified as its embodiment and source. The listed alternatives are mostly differences of emphasis (present vs. future, gift vs. Person, quality vs. duration) rather than mutually exclusive readings. The main genuine divergence is between the theological/symbolic sense and the OT anthropological sense (breath/soul), which coexist in scholarship. Because the bare term 'life' spans many biblical contexts (tree of life, book of life, bread of life, blood as life), interpreters typically specify the context; the Johannine 'the life' formula is the anchor for the dominant reading."}
